speaker: Max Levchin
title: Max Levchin - Building Affirm, PayPal, and Why He Only Starts Network Businesses
question: In software engineering organizations, why do major AI coding productivity gains typically fail to shrink engineering headcount?
guest: Every quarter during planning, we make a long list of things we really want to build, mostly recycled from last quarter's list we didn't get to. Then we draw a red line through it, and everything below the red line gets kicked to the next quarter because we only have so many engineers. Our engineers are all using AI—essentially all pull requests are now AI assisted—and all that's done is push the red line down, so more gets done this quarter instead of kicked down the line. We sort our project list by expected return on investment: we spend dollars on engineers, factor token spend into that cost—since tokens can become a significant part of your cost—and expect revenue dollars out. The world where your list is 1,000 items, you normally fit 200 in, and at the same price you can now do 300 and get more revenue faster—saying "nah, let's cut the engineering team and do 100" is completely counterintuitive. If you're running a company where you're sure there's nothing left to build, you probably should look for someone else to run it.

points.core: Healthy engineering teams always maintain a project backlog far exceeding quarterly capacity.
points.note: Accept: noting that companies continuously have far more valuable projects to build than available engineering bandwidth each planning cycle. Do not credit: generic claims that software is never finished without backlog-capacity dynamics.

points.core: AI productivity lowers the quarterly cutoff to ship more ROI-positive projects faster.
points.note: Accept: explaining that higher output lets the same budget complete further down the ROI-ranked roadmap (e.g., 300 projects instead of 200) to accelerate revenue. Do not credit: vague statements that AI makes engineers more productive.

points.core: Companies evaluate AI coding tools by factoring token spend into engineering ROI.
points.note: Accept: noting that inference/token costs become a material cost line evaluated alongside engineer salaries against expected revenue return. Do not credit: generic claims that AI tools cost money.

points.core: Cutting engineers instead of shipping more only happens when leadership lacks ideas.
points.note: Accept: stating that reducing headcount in response to productivity gains assumes there is nothing worthwhile left to build, signaling a leadership or vision failure. Do not credit: generic optimism about human creativity.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because writing code was never the binding constraint, and because demand for software expands when it gets cheaper.

Coding is only a fraction of an engineer's time, often estimated at a quarter to a third. The rest goes to clarifying requirements, design, code review, testing, debugging, deployment, incident response and coordination. Speeding up one stage shifts the bottleneck elsewhere (Amdahl's law): more generated code means more to review, verify, integrate and maintain, so end-to-end gains are much smaller than task-level gains.

Second, most organizations have a backlog far larger than their capacity. When the cost of building drops, they don't do the same work with fewer people; they pursue more features, products and previously uneconomical projects. This is the Jevons paradox: efficiency raises total consumption.

Third, competitors get the same tools, so gains are spent on keeping pace rather than cutting costs.

Finally, engineers are retained for judgment, system knowledge and accountability for what ships, none of which the tools replace.

Effects do appear at the margins, such as slower hiring or fewer junior roles, rather than proportional headcount cuts.

points.why: The candidate explicitly identifies a project backlog that exceeds available engineering capacity.
quotes: most organizations have a backlog far larger than their capacity

points.why: The candidate says lower costs make more projects viable but leaves out how higher throughput advances projects on the ROI-ranked roadmap and brings returns forward.
The candidate omits token or inference spending from the engineering ROI calculation.
The candidate does not connect cutting headcount to a leadership failure to identify worthwhile projects.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Major AI coding gains rarely shrink engineering headcount because software organizations face elastic demand, non-coding bottlenecks, and competitive pressure. Most companies sit on an effectively infinite backlog of features, technical debt, security hardening, and product experiments. By Jevons paradox, lowering the cost of producing code makes previously marginal projects economically viable, prompting leadership to expand scope rather than cut staff. 

Furthermore, Amdahl’s law limits end-to-end organizational speedup: writing code accounts for only a fraction of an engineer’s work. Requirements gathering, system design, cross-team alignment, code review, testing, deployment, and production operations remain human-intensive bottlenecks. In fact, higher AI code volume often increases downstream demand for human verification, architectural governance, and debugging of subtle integration and reliability issues. 

Finally, because competitors adopt the same AI tools, market expectations rise in lockstep. Any company that uses AI solely to deliver a static roadmap with fewer engineers risks losing ground to rivals that reinvest their newfound capacity into shipping faster, iterating more frequently, and building more ambitious products.

points.why: An effectively infinite backlog of concrete engineering work implies that demand persistently exceeds available capacity in each planning cycle.
quotes: Most companies sit on an effectively infinite backlog of features, technical debt, security hardening, and product experiments.

points.why: The response explains that teams retain staff and use the extra capacity to ship faster and take on projects that have become economically viable.
quotes: lowering the cost of producing code makes previously marginal projects economically viable, prompting leadership to expand scope rather than cut staff.
reinvest their newfound capacity into shipping faster, iterating more frequently, and building more ambitious products.

points.why: The response does not mention token or inference spending as a cost weighed alongside engineering labor against expected returns.
The response frames cutting staff to deliver a static roadmap as a competitive risk without tying that decision to a lack of worthwhile ideas or a failure of leadership vision.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because writing code was never the main constraint. Developers spend only a minority of their time actually typing code. The rest goes to clarifying requirements, design, code review, testing, debugging, integration, deployment, on-call work and coordination. By Amdahl's law, speeding up the coding part alone barely changes total throughput, and the bottleneck simply moves to review, QA and decision-making. AI-generated code can even make those stages heavier.

Demand for software is also highly elastic, a Jevons-paradox effect. Most organizations have backlogs that never run out, so cheaper engineering means building more features, products and experiments, not doing the same work with fewer people. Competitors get the same tools, which pushes firms to spend the gains on keeping up rather than cutting costs.

Measured gains are often smaller than people think. Controlled studies, such as METR's 2025 trial with experienced open-source developers, have found modest or even negative effects on complex, mature codebases. More code also means more to maintain, secure and understand. Finally, layoffs come with organizational friction and risk, so companies more often slow hiring than cut existing staff.

points.why: The persistent backlog supplies worthwhile work beyond what teams can currently deliver.
quotes: Most organizations have backlogs that never run out, so cheaper engineering means building more features, products and experiments

points.why: The response predicts more output but omits the mechanism of moving down an ROI-ranked roadmap to ship valuable projects sooner.
The response does not account for token or inference costs alongside salaries and expected revenue.
The response does not link headcount cuts to leadership running out of worthwhile projects.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Major AI coding gains rarely shrink engineering headcount because software organizations operate with virtually unlimited backlogs and tight downstream bottlenecks. Under Jevons paradox, when writing code becomes faster and cheaper, projects that were previously too costly—such as internal tools, edge-case features, migrations, and long-deferred technical debt—suddenly become worthwhile, expanding total demand for engineering work rather than exhausting it. Just as importantly, writing code accounts for only a small fraction of the software development lifecycle. By Amdahl’s law, speeding up code generation leaves non-coding work—requirements discovery, system design, cross-team coordination, security, deployment, and incident response—as the primary constraints. In fact, higher code volume often increases the burden on code review, testing, and long-term maintenance, requiring experienced engineers to verify and govern AI-generated output. Finally, because competitors adopt the same tools, companies face strong pressure to reinvest productivity gains into faster delivery, better reliability, and new products rather than cutting staff and losing market position.

points.why: The response describes a persistent backlog that exceeds available delivery capacity.
quotes: software organizations operate with virtually unlimited backlogs and tight downstream bottlenecks

points.why: The response explains why cheaper coding makes more work worthwhile, but does not explain how the same budget moves the quarterly cutoff down an ROI-ranked backlog.
The response never discusses token or inference costs as part of engineering ROI.
The response cites competitive pressure to retain staff without linking headcount cuts to a leadership failure to identify worthwhile projects.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Engineering headcount depends on how much work a company wants done, and making software cheaper to build often increases that demand. Most teams already have a backlog of features, reliability fixes, and internal tools. When AI frees up engineering time, projects that were too expensive become worthwhile, and teams can ship more with the same people.

Even large gains in writing code translate into smaller gains across the whole job. Engineers still have to decide what to build, coordinate across teams, review changes, and operate production systems. As coding gets faster, those other activities can become the bottleneck.

Headcount can shrink when demand is fixed or leadership prioritizes cost savings. Where demand is growing, the same gains are more likely to show up as more output or slower hiring.

points.why: The response identifies an existing backlog but never establishes that worthwhile projects routinely far exceed quarterly engineering capacity.
The response explains how AI lowers the threshold for economically worthwhile projects, allowing the same team to ship additional work.
quotes: When AI frees up engineering time, projects that were too expensive become worthwhile, and teams can ship more with the same people.

points.why: The response omits inference costs and their role in calculating engineering ROI.
The response treats cost savings as an independent reason to cut headcount and never links that choice to a leadership failure to identify worthwhile projects.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Major AI coding gains usually change how much an engineering team can deliver before they change how many engineers it needs. Writing code is only part of the job. Even when implementation gets much faster, engineers still have to decide what to build, verify that it works, integrate it with existing systems, and keep it running.

Headcount also depends on how much software an organization wants. Companies often have a backlog of valuable work that was too expensive to justify. When AI lowers the cost of building a feature or fixing a long-standing problem, managers can put the same team to work on more of that backlog. The result may be more output or slower hiring. Headcount is more likely to fall when the workload stays fixed and AI reduces the total engineering effort needed to deliver it.

The response says the same team can tackle more backlog work but does not explain how AI moves the cutoff down an ROI-ranked roadmap to bring forward returns.
The response does not mention token or inference costs as part of engineering ROI.
